title: The Wharf Built with Stolen Stones
hook: One evening in Boston, a boy marshalled his friends to haul away a builder's heap of stones, and by morning they had a neat little fishing wharf standing in the salt marsh. The workmen noticed. Franklin argued the wharf was useful; his father was not persuaded.
counterintuition: Franklin opens his life story by admitting he is writing partly out of vanity — and then defends vanity as "often productive of good," something a man might reasonably thank God for. He treats the trait most memoirists strain to hide as a working asset.
keyTakeaway: A good result does not sanctify a bad method: nothing is truly useful that is not honest.
tryThisNow: At your next meal or meeting with other people, arrive with one genuinely interesting question and steer the talk to it, the way Josiah Franklin seeded his dinner table with a useful topic. Notice how much better the conversation goes than if you'd let it drift.

breakdown.fastRead:
In 1771, on a week's holiday at an English bishop's country house, a sixty-five-year-old Benjamin Franklin sat down to write his life for his son. He begins with genealogy: three hundred years of Franklins at Ecton in Northamptonshire, blacksmiths on thirty acres, and the discovery that he was "the youngest son of the youngest son for five generations back." There is an uncle who invented his own shorthand, and a great-great-grandfather who read a forbidden English Bible taped inside an upturned stool while a child watched the door.

Then Boston. Ben is pulled from grammar school after less than a year because college is too expensive, fails at arithmetic, and is set to cutting candlewick at ten. He wants the sea; his father says no. The chapter's sharpest scene is the stolen stones: Franklin organizes a raid on a builder's stone pile to construct a fishing wharf, pleads the usefulness of the work, and is taught that "nothing was useful which was not honest."
breakdown.deepRead:
The Autobiography begins as a letter. In 1771, staying at Twyford with the Bishop of St. Asaph and expecting "a week's uninterrupted leisure," Franklin started writing his life for his son. His stated reason is almost embarrassingly practical: "Having emerged from the poverty and obscurity in which I was born and bred, to a state of affluence and some degree of reputation in the world," he thought his descendants might like to know the means he used, since some might suit their own situations. He adds that if offered the chance to live it again he would take it, asking only "the advantages authors have in a second edition to correct some faults of the first." And then he confesses that vanity is part of the motive — and defends it, noting drily that he has scarcely ever heard the words "Without vanity I may say" without some vain thing following immediately after.

The ancestry section is not filler; it is a portrait of the stock he came from. Franklins had lived at Ecton in Northamptonshire for three hundred years on about thirty acres, with the smith's trade passed to the eldest son each generation. Poking through the parish registers, which begin in 1555, Franklin found he was "the youngest son of the youngest son for five generations back." His uncle Thomas rose from smith to scrivener and became a public-spirited man of the county; he died exactly four years to the day before Franklin was born, which prompted Franklin's son to say that had the dates matched, "one might have supposed a transmigration." Uncle Benjamin invented his own shorthand, filled volumes with sermons taken down in it, and taught the system to his namesake, who never practised and promptly forgot it.

The family's dissenting streak runs deep. Under Queen Mary they hid an English Bible taped open inside an upturned joint-stool, with a child posted at the door to watch for the church officer. Later, banned conventicles pushed Josiah Franklin to New England around 1682. He fathered seventeen children in all; Franklin remembered thirteen at the table at once.

Boston schooling was brief. Ben went to grammar school at eight, intended for the Church, rose to the head of his class in under a year — and was pulled out when his father weighed the cost of college against the thin livings it produced. At Mr. Brownell's writing school he learned a fair hand but, in his own flat admission, "I failed in the arithmetic, and made no progress in it." At ten he was cutting wick in his father's soap and candle shop, hating it, longing for the sea.

The chapter's best story is the wharf. Franklin led his friends in carrying off a heap of stones meant for a new house and built a place to fish from. Caught, he argued the wharf's usefulness. His father's reply became a rule for life: "nothing was useful which was not honest."
breakdown.fullRead:
The most famous American memoir opens as a private letter. In 1771 Franklin was sixty-five, in England, staying at Twyford at the country house of the Bishop of St. Asaph, with what he expected to be "a week's uninterrupted leisure." He sat down and wrote "Dear son." The tone is a man leaning back after dinner, and the reasons he gives for writing are refreshingly unpious. He had collected anecdotes of his own ancestors with pleasure and assumed his son would enjoy the same about him. And there was the arc worth explaining: "Having emerged from the poverty and obscurity in which I was born and bred, to a state of affluence and some degree of reputation in the world," he thought his posterity might want to know the means he used, since some might prove "fit to be imitated."

Then come two of the most characteristic sentences in the book. Reflecting on how well his life had gone, he says he would happily live it over from the beginning, asking only "the advantages authors have in a second edition to correct some faults of the first" — the printer's mind applied to a human life. And he owns up, cheerfully, to writing partly out of vanity, since denying it would convince nobody. He has scarcely ever heard the preface "Without vanity I may say" without some vain thing arriving directly behind it. Rather than scourge himself, he makes a case: vanity is often productive of good to the man who has it and to those around him, so it would not be absurd to thank God for it among the other comforts of life. Whether you buy the argument or not, it tells you what kind of narrator you have.

The genealogy that follows is not throat-clearing; it is Franklin showing his stock. From notes given him by an uncle with the same taste for family anecdote, he learned the Franklins had lived in the village of Ecton in Northamptonshire for three hundred years, on a freehold of about thirty acres, supported by the smith's trade, which passed to the eldest son every generation. Searching the parish registers — which begin only in 1555, none having been kept before — he made a discovery he clearly enjoyed: "I was the youngest son of the youngest son for five generations back." His grandfather Thomas, born 1598, lived at Ecton until he grew too old for business, then moved to Banbury to live with his son John, a dyer, under whom Josiah Franklin served his apprenticeship. Franklin saw the old man's gravestone in 1758.

Of his grandfather's four surviving sons, two get real portraits. Thomas was bred a smith but, encouraged in learning by an Esquire Palmer, qualified as a scrivener, became a considerable man in the county, was "a chief mover of all public-spirited undertakings" for Northampton and his own village, and was taken up by Lord Halifax. He died on 6 January 1702, old style — four years to the day before Franklin was born. When they heard old people at Ecton describe Thomas's character, Franklin's son remarked that had the death fallen on the same day, "one might have supposed a transmigration."

Uncle Benjamin, the one Franklin was named for, actually lived with the family in Boston for some years. He was a silk dyer trained in London, pious, a devoted sermon-goer, and a political enthusiast — "too much, perhaps, for his station." He left two quarto volumes of his own occasional poetry. He also invented a shorthand of his own and taught it to his young namesake, who never practised and, he admits, has now forgotten it entirely. There is a lovely coda: a London book dealer who knew Franklin as a customer turned up with Uncle Benjamin's collection of political pamphlets running from 1641 to 1717, still eight folio volumes and twenty-four smaller ones, marginal notes and all, apparently left behind when he sailed for America half a century earlier.

The family had been early Protestants, and under Queen Mary they kept an English Bible fastened open with tapes inside the cover of a joint-stool. Franklin's great-great-grandfather would turn the stool upside down on his knees and read to the household, turning the leaves under the tapes, while one of the children stood at the door to watch for the apparitor, the officer of the church court. If he appeared, the stool went back on its feet, Bible hidden. Two generations later the pressure ran the other way: when nonconformist meetings were forbidden and broken up, Benjamin and Josiah stuck with the outed ministers, and around 1682 Josiah carried his wife and three children to New England, where such men expected to worship freely. He had four more children by that wife, and ten by his second, Abiah Folger — seventeen in all, thirteen of whom Franklin remembered sitting at the table at one time. Abiah's father, Peter Folger, appears in Cotton Mather's church history as "a godly, learned Englishman," and wrote a 1675 verse pamphlet arguing for liberty of conscience for Baptists and Quakers, signing it because, as he put it, "to be a libeller (says he) I hate it with my heart."

Ben was sent to grammar school at eight, meant to be the tithe of his father's sons, given to the Church. He had read so early that "I do not remember when I could not read." In under a year he climbed from the middle of his class to the top and was moved up. Then Josiah did the arithmetic on a college education against the number of mouths at his table and the thin livings that many educated men ended up with — reasons Franklin heard him give his friends — and moved the boy to Mr. George Brownell's school for writing and arithmetic, a teacher famous for "mild, encouraging methods." Franklin got a fair hand there. He is blunt about the rest: "I failed in the arithmetic, and made no progress in it." At ten he came home to the candle shop, cutting wick, filling moulds, minding the counter, running errands.

He hated it and wanted the sea; his father flatly refused. So the boy took to the water sideways — swimming well early, handling boats, and noticing that in any difficulty he was "commonly allowed to govern." Which brings the stones. Beside the mill-pond lay a salt marsh where the boys stood at high water to fish for minnows, and their trampling had turned it to a quagmire. Franklin's proposal was a wharf, and he had spotted the materials: a large heap of stones meant for a new house nearby. In the evening, the workmen gone, he assembled his playfellows, and "working with them diligently like so many emmets," sometimes two or three to a stone, they carried off the lot and built their little wharf. Morning brought surprise, inquiry, discovery, complaint, and several fathers correcting several sons. Franklin pleaded the usefulness of the work. His father's answer outlasted the wharf: "nothing was useful which was not honest." He offers the episode as evidence of "an early projecting public spirit, tho' not then justly conducted" — the instinct right, the execution stolen.

The chapter closes with his parents, and the affection is plain. Josiah was middle-sized, strong, ingenious, could draw, could play psalm tunes on his violin and sing to them in the evening after the day's work, which Franklin found extremely agreeable. His real gift was judgment: never employed in public affairs, kept close to his trade by a large family and narrow means, yet constantly visited by leading men wanting his opinion on town or church business, and often chosen as arbitrator between quarrelling parties. At table he liked a sensible friend present and always started some useful topic to improve his children's minds, while nobody discussed the food — with the result that Franklin grew up so indifferent to what he ate that he could scarcely say a few hours after dinner what he had dined on, a convenience in travel that his more discriminating companions never enjoyed.

His mother Abiah nursed all ten of her children. Neither parent was ever ill except in their final illness; he died at 89, she at 85, and they lie together in Boston under a stone their youngest son paid for. Its inscription is the chapter in miniature: without an estate or any gainful employment, by constant labour and industry, they maintained a large family comfortably. "From this instance, reader, Be encouraged to diligence in thy calling, And distrust not Providence."

examples.title: The spreadsheet nobody approved
examples.scenario: Marisol coordinates shifts for four branches of a regional bakery. The official scheduling system can't handle swaps, so staff text her at midnight and things get lost. Over a weekend she exports the full staff list — names, phone numbers, contracted hours — out of the HR system she has read access to, and builds a shared swap sheet. It works beautifully. Absences drop. Nobody asked her permission to pull that data, and nobody has told the staff their numbers are now in a spreadsheet three managers can open.
examples.whatToDo: Before you roll it out further, take the tool to whoever owns the data and ask for it properly, showing the results as your argument. If the answer is no, rebuild it on data people have actually consented to share.
examples.whyItMatters: A working solution built on a quiet violation stays fragile forever — it can be killed the moment it's noticed, and the person who built it absorbs the blame. Usefulness is a reason to get permission, not a substitute for it.

examples.title: The bio you keep deleting
examples.scenario: Tomasz has redrafted his illustrator bio eleven times for a gallery's group show. Every version that mentions the national prize, the two book covers, or the eight years of teaching gets cut by morning because it reads, to him, as showing off. What's left is three lines so modest that visitors will assume he's an amateur. The gallery's copy deadline is Thursday, and the blandest draft is currently the one in the folder.
examples.whatToDo: Write the accurate version — prize, covers, years taught — and let it stand, on the grounds that these are facts a reader needs, not boasts. Ask one honest friend to flag anything that's actually inflated rather than merely flattering.
examples.whyItMatters: Refusing to state your record isn't humility; it's transferring the work of judging you onto people who have no information. Plain accuracy about yourself is more trustworthy than performed smallness.

examples.title: Recording your grandfather's stories
examples.scenario: Aneta has started recording her grandfather, a retired machinist, on Sunday afternoons. He tells the same story about the flooded workshop in 1974 three weeks running and the year changes each time — 1974, then 1972, then "the year your mother started school." Aneta has begun quietly correcting him, which makes him stop talking. She has eleven hours of audio and no idea which parts she could defend to a skeptical cousin.
examples.whatToDo: Stop correcting mid-story; let him finish, then ask what else was happening that year. In your notes, mark each claim as confirmed, uncertain, or contradicted, and keep the uncertain ones with the flag attached rather than dropping them.
examples.whyItMatters: An account that admits where it's shaky is more useful than one that sounds uniformly confident, because a reader can tell which parts to lean on. Flagging doubt preserves the story instead of forcing a choice between silence and false precision.

questions.prompt: Why did Josiah Franklin take his son out of grammar school after less than a year?
choices: Benjamin had fallen behind the rest of his class and was unlikely to keep up
Uncle Benjamin withdrew his offer of the shorthand sermon volumes
He weighed the expense of a college education against the poor livings many educated men obtained
The family was preparing to leave Boston and return to Northamptonshire
questions.explanation: Franklin says his father changed his mind "from a view of the expense of a college education, which having so large a family he could not well afford, and the mean living many so educated were afterwards able to obtain." Far from falling behind, Ben had risen from the middle of his class to the head of it.

questions.prompt: What did Franklin and his playfellows use to build their wharf on the salt marsh?
choices: A heap of stones set aside for a new house being built near the marsh
Timber left over from his father's candle and soap workshop
Barrels and planks taken from a boat moored on the mill-pond
Bricks salvaged from a wall that had fallen during the winter
questions.explanation: Franklin showed his comrades "a large heap of stones, which were intended for a new house near the marsh," and they carried them off in the evening after the workmen had gone.

questions.prompt: How does Franklin treat his own vanity in the opening of the Autobiography?
choices: He denies it firmly, insisting he writes only for his son's instruction
He apologizes for it and promises the reader he has since overcome it
He blames it on the flattery of friends who urged him to write
He confesses it and argues it is often productive of good to its possessor and to others
questions.explanation: Franklin admits the confession since "my denial of it will be believed by nobody," then defends vanity as often useful — so much so that "it would not be altogether absurd if a man were to thank God for his vanity among the other comforts of life."

questions.prompt: What became of the shorthand system that Uncle Benjamin taught young Franklin?
choices: Franklin used it for decades to record sermons and public speeches
Franklin never practised it and had forgotten it by the time he wrote
Franklin improved on it and published it under his own name in London
Franklin lost the key to it when his uncle's papers went missing
questions.explanation: Franklin writes that his uncle "had formed a short-hand of his own, which he taught me, but, never practising it, I have now forgot it" — one of several plain admissions of his own lapses in this chapter.

questions.prompt: A volunteer group improves a neglected public path by taking gravel from an unattended council depot. When challenged, they point to the finished path and the people now using it. What does this chapter's lesson suggest?
choices: The finished path settles the matter; results are the only fair test of an action
They should keep the path quiet and avoid drawing official attention to it
The good of the path doesn't excuse taking the gravel — the means have to be honest too
They were right to act, since asking permission would only have slowed the work
questions.explanation: Franklin pleaded exactly this defence — the usefulness of the wharf — and his father "convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest." Franklin keeps the good instinct but calls the execution "not then justly conducted."

questions.prompt: A team lead wants meetings that actually teach people something. Which practice most closely follows Josiah Franklin's example at his dinner table?
choices: Letting conversation run freely so the most urgent topic surfaces on its own
Arriving with one useful question prepared and deliberately steering talk toward it
Asking each person in turn to report on their own week in a fixed order
Keeping talk light so that nobody feels tested in front of colleagues
questions.explanation: Josiah "always took care to start some ingenious or useful topic for discourse, which might tend to improve the minds of his children" — a topic chosen in advance rather than left to chance.

reviewCards.front: What lesson did Franklin's father draw from the stolen stones?
reviewCards.back: That "nothing was useful which was not honest" — the wharf's usefulness didn't excuse how the materials were got.

reviewCards.front: Where and when did Franklin begin the Autobiography, and to whom is it addressed?
reviewCards.back: At Twyford in 1771, at the Bishop of St. Asaph's country house, during a week's leisure. It's written as a letter to his son.

reviewCards.front: What did Franklin find in the Ecton parish registers about his own place in the family?
reviewCards.back: That he was "the youngest son of the youngest son for five generations back." The registers went back only to 1555.

reviewCards.front: How did Franklin's family hide their English Bible under Queen Mary?
reviewCards.back: Taped open inside the cover of a joint-stool, read with the stool turned upside down on the reader's knees, while a child watched the door for the apparitor.

reviewCards.front: Name two things Franklin admits he failed at or lost in this chapter.
reviewCards.back: He failed at arithmetic under Mr. Brownell and made no progress in it, and he forgot Uncle Benjamin's shorthand for lack of practice.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Test a good idea twice — once for whether it works, and once for whether the way you got there is honest. Pair that with the habit of assessing yourself plainly, neither inflating nor deleting the record.

ifThenPlans.context: When you catch yourself justifying a shortcut by pointing at the result it produced
ifThenPlans.plan: Then pause and name the specific permission, rule, or person you went around, and either get it squared or rebuild the thing without it.

ifThenPlans.context: When you're about to cut a true fact about your own work because it sounds like bragging
ifThenPlans.plan: Then keep it if it's accurate and a reader needs it, and cut only what you can't actually support.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one thing you've built or arranged on an unofficial shortcut — an export, an access you were never granted, a favour never cleared — and either regularize it today or write down the exact step that would.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, bring one prepared, genuinely interesting question to a meal or meeting and steer the conversation to it, the way Josiah Franklin seeded his table. Note afterwards what came out of it that wouldn't have otherwise.

memorableLines.text: though I pleaded the usefulness of the work, mine convinced me that nothing was useful which was not honest
Most people dislike vanity in others, whatever share they have of it themselves; but I give it fair quarter wherever I meet with it

were it offered to my choice, I should have no objection to a repetition of the same life from its beginning, only asking the advantages authors have in a second edition to correct some faults of the first
